## Session 90 — EVERY GAME EVERY MAN EVER PLAYS IS NOW KEPT, FOREVER. Before this session the engine forgot a game the instant it finished: season totals survived, the games that made them did not, and a player who never got off the bench left no trace at all. S90 gives a career a permanent archive. Bound to a history file, a season now writes one log holding two things — **who was on every roster that year** (name, school, position, archetype, recruiting rank and all 38 ratings, including the 661 men who never played a minute) and **one row per man per game he played**, twenty-one counters each. Read it back and you have his stats, his career highs, his game-by-game log, for as long as the file exists. Emmett's framing, which decided the scope: *"I just want the player card to be a historical record that persists long after they've graduated… his recruiting ranking, his career highs, his full college stats, game by game log."* **The archive records what happened, not what might have.** ★ THE FORMAT WAS SHAPED MORE BY WHAT IT REFUSED THAN BY WHAT IT STORES. Three claims that four prompt revisions had carried were false against the source and were caught before the bytes hardened: the row was missing a counter the engine already attributes (the offensive foul, dropped by the season line since S87 — O-67); the world fingerprint is not 32 raw bytes but a labelled string, so its label check can only live at the writer; and the "compact JSON is 5–8× the size" argument that justified a custom binary format is **wrong by most of an order of magnitude** — measured, it is a wash. The format survived on different grounds. **Verified on Emmett's machine: ALL CHECKS PASSED, Phase 81 PASS at 41 assertions, and the season page byte-identical to its pre-S90 self with zero new lines.** The stock season's log is 21,162,128 bytes — 4,511 roster entries, 5,205 game blocks, **105,830 rows** — matching the predicted size to the byte. (2026-08-02)

**Register:** build. Eight new files (five in `Charm.History`: the layout, writer, reader, refusal enum and history schema v2; two in the harness: the retention layer and Phase 81; plus a golden fixture), seven edited. Gate 1 baselines banked before the build; Gate 2 check-in ran against the pulled tree; the prompt went through five ChatGPT review passes (r1→r7, ~90 findings).

### What is stored, and the two rulings that decided it

- **R7 — the archive stores who he WAS, not only what he did** (Emmett). Game rows say nothing about a man, and a man who never played has no rows, so without a roster section he would not exist in the archive at all. Hence one entry per man per season, written before the first tip.
- **R8 — ratings are stamped at the START of the season.** Inert today (nobody develops mid-season); fixed now because the FORMAT is fixed now. The card should read as one coherent thing — *this is who he was, this is what he did.* End-of-season stamping would show what he grew into beside statistics he produced as somebody else.
- **★ The ceiling is OUT** (Emmett, ruling on §0c): *"No, 10 years down the line, it doesn't matter. It should maintain a historical record."* A ceiling is a scouting opinion about a future that did not occur. **Arrival went with it** — it is defined as a fraction OF the ceiling and would be permanently uninterpretable stored alone. That consequence was surfaced rather than assumed.

### ★ The finding the audits were built to catch: a counter the season line had been dropping

The engine has named the man who takes a charge since S87. `SeasonPlayerRecord` never picked the column up — it was summed league-wide only. **Conservation could never have found it**: conservation compares the row to the season record, and the record is the thing that was already missing it, so a subset was being compared to itself. It was found by auditing the row against `PlayerBoxTotals` — what the ENGINE attributes — instead. The rule now stands in the prompt: *audit against the engine's attribution, never against the layer you are copying from.*

It matters permanently because of the retention ruling: **a primitive not tracked at write time cannot be recreated for a game already written.** Adding it after one season had been archived would have meant that season never has it. The field was added; the printed column was deliberately NOT (the page must stay byte-identical), so O-67 stays open.

Its determinism coverage is mandatory, and the discriminating check is a negative control that **moves one offensive foul between two men on the same team, leaving the league total unchanged**, and requires the check to go red. A league-total check cannot see that — the S81 lesson about building the check that discriminates on the axis the change is about.

### The shape

The durable unit is one GAME. Rows are built and validated in memory, serialized whole, appended in one write — and that write is **not** claimed to be physically atomic. Safety comes from framing: a partial write leaves an incomplete final block and the reader refuses to expose it as complete, so a structurally valid half-game cannot exist. Sections carry their own checksums; the footer carries a digest of everything after the file header.

**A row is born by SNAPSHOT AND DIFF, not a second accumulator** — re-implementing attribution is exactly how a game log and a season line drift apart. Two details are load-bearing and were confirmed against source at check-in:

- **The boundary is the whole loop iteration, and the ORDER matters.** The season loop calls `Accumulate` → `AccumulateFouling` → `NoteOccupancy`; box fields land in the first, credits and the on-floor denominators in the third. A boundary drawn between them silently drops every counter of one kind, and every check would still pass.
- **26 men, not 4,511.** Only this game's two rosters can move, provable because both writes reach the record through one resolver that indexes this game's rows. The r4 draft snapshotted the whole league 5,205 times a season for nothing.

**Emission is the games-played delta**, never inferred from a credits delta afterwards — a second definition of "played" beside the real one. And **a counter moving for a man who did not play is a hard error** that stops the run. That check is the only proof that the participation predicate and the accumulator agree about who was on the floor; everything else about it was an argument.

### ★ Where the codec lives was decided by S89's seam, not by preference

Writing a `PersonId` to disk needs its raw number, which is `internal` to `Charm.History` with no `InternalsVisibleTo`. A codec in the harness cannot compile without opening that wall. **The seam also held against the tests** — Phase 81 cannot mint identities and takes them from a real allocator instead — and it forced two shapes that turned out right for other reasons: the public surface is DTOs, and **the writer sorts both sections itself**, because `PersonId` deliberately has no ordering and the harness physically cannot hand them over sorted.

One door was opened and is named rather than slipped in: a **public** test-only hook pinning the career's lineage label. The migration golden has no other honest form — production mints from `Guid.NewGuid()`, so a v1→v2 migration produces a different file every run. It hands out no identity value, so the real seam is untouched.

### History schema v2 — the career lineage

Two careers started from the same world legally share the world fingerprint AND start at person 1, season 1, game 1, so a log copied between them would pass every check v1 could make. `historyId` closes it. **A history created after S90 is born v2**; a pre-S90 file migrates once, atomically, under the lock already held, with every counter carried across untouched. The migration falsified `HistoryStore.Open`'s own doc comment (which promised opening writes nothing) and it was corrected with the code.

**What it does NOT prove, stated rather than implied:** a history CLONED at the filesystem carries its label, so those branches are indistinguishable — the same trust boundary S89 already draws, since a clone also duplicates every counter.

### The struck argument

r4 justified the custom binary format by claiming compact JSON would be 5–8× the bytes. Measured on realistic rows: **20.18 MiB binary against 19.8–21.9 MiB for text, and omit-the-zeros JSON is SMALLER.** A per-game row is mostly zeros and single digits; a fixed-width row spends eight bytes on each regardless. The format stands on what survived — predictable index targets for a future almanac, exact size arithmetic assertable to the byte, and zero dependencies — and the seek claim was narrowed too: fixed width gives O(1) access to a *known* offset, not O(1) career lookup, which still needs an index nobody has built.

An earlier revision also asserted "the measured 105,830 rows." **That number was the seat-occupancy count, not a row count**, and was an upper bound. The true count was measured at the end and came in at exactly 105,830 — the two populations coincide, so every man who held a seat played at least one possession. The bound was tight; the claim was still wrong when it was made.

### Three things the build caught that reasoning had not

1. **Phase 80's B10 went correctly red.** It asserts a new history matches the committed golden, and new histories are now v2. Retargeted, and the v2 golden emitted through the production writer rather than typed.
2. **Two seasons of one career cannot share an open store** — S89 closes reservations before the simulation on purpose. The first version of A8 shared one and crashed. The allocator was right; the test was wrong, and the fix (reopen the career between seasons) is the faithful shape anyway.
3. **Overflow refuses before the file exists.** A13 promised no artifact after an overlong name, but the writer created the file first. The state machine now begins at `RosterPrepared`, a pure in-memory stage with no filesystem contact.

### Known gaps, named not buried

**O-72** — class year exists on the generated player and is dropped before the season; not stored, because Emmett did not name it. **O-73** — the generator computes a development ceiling for all 4,511 men every world build and `GenMapToPlayer` discards it one line before the season sees it; the retention ruling settles storage, not the engine gap. Two facts worth not re-deriving: the current card is fully redundant with the stored 38, and runway is exactly latent minus current.

**Hierarchy rank is 5 for every player in the league** — nothing sets it. Stored anyway: two bytes, authored surface that will become live, and a season written without it could never get it back.

### One process miss

The prompt carried an "O-number renumber" chore from r4 through r7 and **it does not exist** — no duplicate O-numbers; O-25 is simply a number never assigned. The real collision in the record was S88's phase number, fixed at S89.1. Every code claim around it got the §6b source audit; a chore claim inherited across four revisions got none. **The audit's scope is the whole prompt, not just its claims about code.**

### What S88 actually is, read properly this time

Before S88 a fast break was **one team average against another** — the defence's mean Hustle shaved a couple of points off the make, and that was the entire transition defence. Nobody guarded anybody, and the engine could not tell a break against an elite rim protector from a break against a shooting guard. **It was the last place in the engine where a team was a scalar instead of five men.**

S88 replaces it with a per-man GOT-BACK number — his legs, and how deep the man he is guarding starts — doing three jobs: **who** is the defender on this break, **how set** he is when he arrives, and **how many** of them got back (the dominant channel on conversion, and what the old Hustle wire was reaching for).

Eight rulings are encoded in it, and two are worth repeating here because they are the no-scalar wall holding:

- **R2 — depth is set by THE MAN YOU ARE GUARDING, never by your own body.** Read off the opposing lineup, so a defence is not stranded under the rim against a team that goes small. Reading it off the defender's own size would be a scalar wearing a costume. Phase 79's A9 constructs exactly that mis-wire and proves the real check rejects it: five identical defenders collapse to one identical number, where the correct wire gives 1.5495 / 1.4575 / 1.2803 / 1.0383 / 0.9186.
- **R6 — Hustle rides INSIDE the legs term** and gets no channel of its own. Keeping both would pay a fast, high-effort team twice — the S86 double-count.

Anchoring is exact: five average men on an average offence give an aggregate of **1.000000000000000**, and the break make and block reproduce their configured bases to the digit.

### The four wrong calls S89 made about S88, each with its cause

**The common thread with S89's own four misses is the same reflex:** a plausible cause stated as a finding without opening the thing that would confirm it. S89's misses were sandbox-vs-Windows; these were GitHub-vs-working-directory. Both are *"I looked at a copy and reported on the original."*

### Standing rules this session earns

- **A GitHub pull is not the working directory.** Before asserting that something does not exist, `git status` the whole tree — untracked files are invisible to a zipball, and a bare `git status --short <one path>` hides them too.
- **Never diagnose a red suite from the outside.** Open the failure and read the line before naming a cause. Every wrong call above would have died in ten seconds against the actual output.
- **A new suite phase must be registered AND its fixtures added to the harness project.** S88 did neither and shipped a check file that had never run; S89 collided with its number. A phase that is not in `Program.cs`'s registration block does not exist.

### The shape that shipped

```
src/Charm.History/                       NEW PROJECT — the seam is the assembly boundary
  PersonId.cs  SeasonId.cs  GameId.cs    readonly record structs, private long, internal FromRaw/Raw
  HistoryException.cs                    16 named reasons; tests assert the CODE, never the message
  HistorySchemaV1.cs                     canonical writer + strict loader
  HistoryStore.cs                        sidecar lock, high-water allocator, atomic publish
  PersonIdentityMap.cs                   the frozen bijection + IdentityGuard
```

Three counters and a world binding, and deliberately nothing else:

```json
{ "format": "charm-history", "schemaVersion": 1,
  "worldFingerprint": "sha256-v1:…", "nextPersonId": 1, "nextSeasonId": 1, "nextGameId": 1 }
```

The retention session (O-31) adds the entity tables. What it inherits from here is that every number those tables will store is trustworthy, because nothing was ever reused underneath them.

### ★ WHY HIGH-WATER AND NEVER A FREE LIST

There is no record of which numbers were issued and no way to hand one back. The counters ARE the proof. A scheme that filled holes would have to KNOW which numbers were free, which means a list, which means the list can be wrong — and the failure mode of a wrong list is two men sharing one career. Holes are permanent and cost nothing.

Order per batch is **reserve → make durable → only then hand out**. Backwards would mean a crash between issuing and persisting leaves the file believing those numbers are still available while people are already wearing them. Losing a range to a crash is free; reissuing one is fatal.

The lock is a **sidecar** (`<path>.lock`), not the data file. Holding the data file open exclusively and then atomically replacing that same file does not work on Windows — the replace needs the file not to be held. The lock is taken FIRST, before existence is even checked (checking first is the creation race), and released before the long simulation, which issues nothing.

### ★ WHERE THE THREE KINDS OF NUMBER ARE ISSUED

| kind | where | batch |
|---|---|---|
| person | `BuildDivvyPool`, the ONE construction site | one reservation for all 4,511 |
| season | `BuildSeasonSchedule`, after the slate validates | one |
| game | same place, same write | one block of 5,205 |

The schedule is built identity-free FIRST and validated, and only then numbered. A schedule that fails to build must not already have spent a season number on itself. Once reserved the numbers are durable, so a season that then fails burns them permanently — a gap, never a retry.

**4,511 people in ONE reservation, not 4,511 writes.** Per-player writes would be slow AND would leave 4,510 windows in which a crash strands a partly-numbered pool.

### ★ THE CALL THAT WENT AGAINST THE PROMPT: the number is not on the pool row

A-3 suggested `PersonId` as a new field beside `PoolId` on `PoolPlayer`. It is not there. Phase 54 `with`-clones pool rows in its rigged-pool checks, and an identity riding through a test clone is an identity a helper can duplicate. The frozen `PersonIdentityMap` beside the pool is the only carrier, it is validated as a bijection at construction (no pool slot twice, no person number twice, full coverage), and a lookup miss **throws** — a silently skipped man would leave a whole season of statistics filed nowhere while every conservation total stayed green, because the totals would only ever have counted the men who were found.

`PoolId` is untouched and must stay so: it is **position-encoded** (guards 0–1734, wings 1735–3122, bigs 3123–4510 via `RosterShape.PositionForPoolIndex`). Renumbering it reclassifies the league.

### ★ SCHEDULEFINGERPRINT NEEDED NO CHANGE, AND THAT IS WORTH RECORDING

The prompt's §5.5 warned the fingerprint might absorb the new fixture fields. It never could — it has always hashed index/kind/home/away **by name** rather than letting the record hash itself. That is the only reason `93d8c853…` survives. A property that was already right, recorded in place so a later session does not "tidy" it into default record hashing.

**Every one is the same error: a number computed in Claude's Linux sandbox, asserted against Emmett's Windows machine.** CONVENTIONS §2 has said since S81.3 that a sandbox artifact may not be compared bit-for-bit on Emmett's machine.   World fingerprint: sha256-v1:fa823da9…                             =>

After one season: `nextPersonId 4512, nextSeasonId 2, nextGameId 5206` — one past 4,511 people, one season, 5,205 fixtures. Predicted exactly; these are counts, not arithmetic, so they are machine-independent.

Suite: `ALL CHECKS PASSED`, Phase 79 **71 of 71 green first time**.

### Phase 79 — what actually discriminates

Most of the eleven groups would pass on a broken implementation, because "it did not crash" is cheap. Two cannot:

- **B2, the type surface.** Reflection over all three id types: no ordering/conversion/arithmetic operator exists, no public member returns a numeric primitive (`GetHashCode` exempt **by name**, so a future `public long Value` cannot hide behind the exemption), no `IComparable`, equality operators present and required, `Raw` non-public, and **no `InternalsVisibleTo` on the assembly** — because a friend grant would silently unseal every check above it without changing any of them. This proves the banned operations are *unwritable*, which beats demonstrating one misuse.
- **B8, isolation with a real negative control.** Legacy and history seasons compared across a 17,581-character surface (fingerprint, every result, every standing, five conservation counters, eighteen columns per player-season). Then **one live per-player field is moved by a single shot** and the comparison is required to go red. A string mutation would only have proved two different strings differ; mutating the outcome proves the surface is actually reading the season.

**B1's non-reuse check reads the FILE, not the identities** — deliberately. "The next number is above every prior one" cannot be asserted by comparing identities, because identities cannot be compared; that is the entire point of B2. Non-reuse is read off the persisted counters, which is also the surface that carries the guarantee across a restart.

B10 covers every rejection path with its own classification: malformed JSON, unknown key, missing key, wrong format, unsupported version, wrong type, out-of-domain counter, wrong world, path-is-a-directory, lock held. Each also asserts **the file was not modified**. The check-only helpers build history files BY HAND rather than through the store — a check that could only build a file with the writer could never test what the reader does with a file the writer would not have produced.

### Two design notes for the next session at this seam

**The history is named, never defaulted.** There is deliberately no fallback path. A hidden file appearing next to the binary the first time a season runs is how somebody ends up with three careers they cannot tell apart, and how a throwaway test run permanently burns four thousand person numbers out of a real one. No argument means no history, no file, no allocator — exactly how every session before this one behaved.

**The fingerprint is the WHOLE world, not a chosen subset.** Guessing which fields "can affect generation" is precisely the omission that bites three seasons later when somebody edits a prestige value and the careers quietly continue against a different league. The world is small and does not change; hashing all of it costs nothing and cannot be wrong. A future format change defines `sha256-v2` rather than redefining what v1 meant. Note for the curious: `stock-d1.world.json` currently hashes to the same value as its own canonical projection (`fa823da9…`), because the committed file was writer-produced — a coincidence, not a rule, which is why the fingerprint hashes the parsed model and not the file bytes.

## Session 88 — WHO GOT BACK: THE LAST TEAM-SCALAR IN THE ENGINE IS GONE. Before this session a fast break was ONE TEAM AVERAGE against another — the defence's mean Hustle against the offence's shaved a couple of points off the make, and that was the entire transition defence. Nobody guarded anybody, no individual rating was read, and the engine could not tell a break against an elite rim protector from a break against a shooting guard. **It was the one place left in the engine where a team was a scalar instead of five men.** S88 replaces it with a per-man GOT-BACK number — his legs, and how deep the man he is guarding starts — and that single number does three jobs: **WHO** is the defender on this break, **HOW SET** he is when he arrives, and **HOW MANY** of them got back, which is the dominant channel on conversion and the thing the old Hustle wire was reaching for. Oracle-first, ported constant for constant: `tools/transition_defense_oracle.py` was signed off by Emmett reading its archetype tables, and the C# is held to `emit_golden()` rather than to a re-derivation of the formulas. **The anchor is exact** — five average men against an average offence give an aggregate of `1.000000000000000` and reproduce the configured break make and break block to the digit, so a neutral lineup moves nothing and no config rebase was needed. ★ **THIS ENTRY IS A BACKFILL, WRITTEN AT S90, AND ITS LIMITS ARE WORTH STATING.** S88 shipped without a journal or design entry and its files were untracked, so S89 misread it as an abandoned dial set and reverted its config; S89.1 found the code, restored the config, registered the orphaned suite phase and recorded the correction — but left the subsystem itself undocumented (O-71). What follows is reconstructed from the locked oracle, the source headers and the 910-line check file. **The eight rulings survive verbatim because S88 wrote them into the oracle header; the design conversation that produced them does not survive and is not reconstructed here.** That is the cost of shipping without docs, recorded rather than hidden. (2026-07-31, entered 2026-08-02)

**Register:** build, backfilled. Four new engine files (`TransitionDefense.cs` 279 lines, `TransitionContext.cs`, `TransitionDefenderPicker.cs`, `TransitionContest.cs`), one locked Python oracle plus its golden emitter, two golden fixtures, one 910-line check file with thirteen assertion groups, twenty new `Transition*` config dials replacing four `HustleTransitionDefense*` ones. Live wiring: `RollHGenerator:590` (`BreakMakePct`), `RollHGenerator:689` (`BreakBlockPct`), `Resolver:1329/1337/1339` (`LineupGotBack`, `TeamAggregate`, the defender draw) — roughly 98,000 shots a season.

### The eight rulings, verbatim from the oracle header

These are Emmett's, from the S88 design conversation (2026-07-31), and they are the only surviving record of it.

- **R1 — nobody is ever impossible.** No guarantee how many get back; faster players are MORE LIKELY to be the one there. Hence a luck floor above zero and a weighted draw rather than a threshold.
- **R2 — depth is set by THE MAN YOU ARE GUARDING, never by your own body.** Even five identical rangy athletes have one man playing the five, and he is under the basket; his odds are muted, never zero, and his legs fight it. ★ Read off the OPPOSING lineup, so a defence is not stranded under the rim against a team that goes small — there is no post to be stuck guarding. Reading it off the defender's own size would be **a scalar wearing a costume**, the S81.1 mistake in a new place.
- **R3 — the break block is a CHASE-DOWN.** Speed and length lead; rim protection is the junior partner, not the driver. A rangy fast wing whose block rating gives him nothing in the halfcourt runs people down in transition.
- **R4 — a break stays a better look than a halfcourt set**, even against a good defender, so the defensive read is discounted rather than full strength. But it is not FREE, which is what it was.
- **R5 — being there is worth something ON ITS OWN**, independent of any rating. A guard standing in the lane makes you change the shot even though he will never block it. ★ Without this the design is inert: the first draft scaled arrival by a defender's rim-protection DEVIATION from average, which cancels across a lineup, and whole-team speed moved break FG% by 0.0 points.
- **R6 — Hustle rides INSIDE the legs term** and gets no channel of its own. The old team-mean Hustle wire retires into this; keeping both would pay a fast, high-effort team twice for turning and running — the same double-count that retired two dials at S86.
- **R7 — where he shot from moves him on THIS trip.** A man who just shot at the rim is standing under it; a man who just shot a three is already at the arc, halfway back. **A stretch big is genuinely better transition defence than a back-to-the-basket big of identical speed.**
- **R8 — no discrete "nobody got back" branch.** Every transition iteration lumps into one sum: the 2-on-0 and the 1-on-3 acrobatic finish are already inside the make distribution, and the play-by-play layer names them later from the outcome. **A very weak contest IS the runaway dunk.**

### The shape

A defender's got-back number is a luck floor plus his legs times his depth: legs are speed-primary with hustle riding inside (R6), symmetric about 50; depth is a tanh read of the man he is guarding against that man's OWN lineup's mean post-ness (R2), above 1 on a perimeter man and below 1 on their post. The shooter's zone multiplies the shooter's own defender only (R7). The team aggregate normalises by the occupied count times a league-average reference, which is what makes five average men land on exactly 1.0.

**Two layers on purpose.** The raw numeric primitives take doubles and are what golden parity binds to, so the fixture drives the real code rather than a transcription of it — the same shape as `FoulCommitter`, for the same reason. The Player-facing overloads sit on top and own the one mapping question the oracle does not answer: the oracle's `post` is `Matchup.Postness` and its `length` is `Matchup.LengthRating`, both blends of weights summing to 1.0, so both share the raw 0–99 scale the oracle's constants assume.

**All twenty magnitudes are CALIBRATION PLACEHOLDERS** on `MatchupConfig`. None is ever suite-asserted (page-only calibration principle); the suite asserts parity against the oracle and the wiring invariants, and the numbers live on the season page.

### ★ The check that earns its place: A9, the negative control for R2

A4 asserts that five IDENTICAL defenders produce five DIFFERENT got-back numbers, strictly decreasing in the opponent's post-ness. That check passes on the correct wire and would also pass on several wrong ones, so A9 constructs the specific mis-wire the ruling forbids — depth read off the defender's OWN body — and requires it to collapse five identical defenders to one identical number, where the real wire gives **1.5495 / 1.4575 / 1.2803 / 1.0383 / 0.9186**. It then asserts the real weights differ from the mis-wired ones. This is the S73.1 discipline: an acceptance test of "the right thing happened" paired with a signal only the correct tree can produce.

The other twelve groups: golden parity (228 cases, absolute bound, plus a guard that the fixture's constants still match the live config); the anchor, including a Mid-zone break leaving it untouched and a Three-zone break moving it, so R7 is proven live rather than inert; the aggregate responding to the offence's SHAPE rather than its SIZE, and to WHICH defender is stuck on their big, which a mean of defensive ratings could not do; pairing checks at both the depth component and the full weights, with asymmetric occupancy; the denominator; an occupancy matrix driven through the real generator, including a break with nobody on defence still resolving and the block-credit path still refusing to invent a blocker; and one-axis-at-a-time monotonicity at the parameter interface.

### What S88 did not do, and what it cost

The session shipped code and shipped no documentation, and every downstream problem followed from that single omission. Its files were untracked, so a GitHub pull could not see them; its suite phase was declared but never registered, so it had **no caller anywhere and had never executed once**; its two golden fixtures were never added to the harness project, so those checks could not have passed even if the phase had been wired. S89 then read the tree, found twenty config dials with no code behind them, and reverted a working session's configuration. S89.1 corrected all of it — phase registered at 79 by date, identity moved to 80, both fixtures added, config restored — and its first-ever run went 40 of 43, all three failures the missing fixtures. **The lesson is not "write the docs." It is that an unregistered phase and an untracked file are both forms of code that does not exist**, and neither announces itself: the suite was green throughout, because a check with no caller cannot fail.
